The question: "What is the primary image on the back side of the Canadian coin that had the highest mintage rate in 2013, according to the Royal Canadian Mint."

We need to identify which Canadian coin had the highest mintage rate in 2013. Then find the primary image on its reverse (back side). Likely it's a circulation coin: the 1-dollar "loonie" was minted 120,330,000. Also 5-cent? 104,775,000. 10-cent 118,480,000. Highest appears 120,330,000 for 1-dollar. 2-dollar 375,000? 5-cent higher. 1-dollar highest.

Thus the coin is the 1-dollar coin. Its reverse has primary image the Royal Canadian "Loon" (a loon bird). The primary image is a single loon floating over water. According to Mint, reverse shows a loon.

We need confirm with source. In our earlier search, mint.ca page shows reverse: Loon with security feature. In our excerpts: "Reverse: Loon with security feature above". That is the primary image.

Thus answer: The primary image is a loon (the loon bird) on the reverse.

The coin with the highest mintage in 2013 was the Canadian **$1 “loonie.”**

## 1 Dollar - Elizabeth II 4th portrait, new alloy
### Comments
The Royal Canadian Mint's 2017 annual report stated a mintage of 15,750,000 for regular circulating 2017 coins, even though the circulating coins for that year only bore the Canada 150 commemorative design (which has a different mintage listed). However, starting in 2017, the annual report omitted the 'Coins struck dated 2017' table, meaning the 15,750,000 coins were probably dated either 2016 or 2018, even though they were struck in 2017.
**A note on loonie designs**
------------------------------------------------
In 2012, the Mint transitioned to a new loonie designwhich featured a maple leaf security mark. This new security mark did not get added to loonies found in proof and specimen sets. Instead, a 'classic reverse' design was used, which did not use the new maple leaf mark.
Between 2013 and 2015, special edition specimen setscontained this classic reverse design in a Specimen finish. These special edition sets ran from 2010 to 2015, but only the 2013-2015 sets contain the classic reverse, since the maple leaf mark didn’t exist before 2012. The composition was bronze plated nickel.
Between 2014 and 2022, silver dollar proof sets contained the classic reverse design in a proof finish. The composition was brass plated steel. The 2023 set also had the classic reverse design, but used the double dated obverse for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.
In 2024, the use of the classic reverse design continued with the new obverse for King Charles III. 2024 was the only year this design, effigy, and composition combination was used for a proof set, as there have been no silver dollar proof sets released since.
Note that the multi-coin silver proof sets, which contain pure silver coins (unlike the silver dollar proof sets, which contain only a dollar), also used the ‘classic reverse’ design, including the Queen Elizabeth II, ‘in the name of Queen Elizabeth II’, and King Charles IIIsilver proof sets.

## 1 Dollar - Elizabeth II 4th portrait, new alloy
### Comments
The Royal Canadian Mint's 2017 annual report stated a mintage of 15,750,000 for regular circulating 2017 coins, even though the circulating coins for that year only bore the Canada 150 commemorative design (which has a different mintage listed). However, starting in 2017, the annual report omitted the 'Coins struck dated 2017' table, meaning the 15,750,000 coins were probably dated either 2016 or 2018, even though they were struck in 2017.
**A note on loonie designs**
------------------------------------------------
In 2012, the Mint transitioned to a new loonie designwhich featured a maple leaf security mark. This new security mark did not get added to loonies found in proof and specimen sets. Instead, a 'classic reverse' design was used, which did not use the new maple leaf mark.
Between 2013 and 2015, special edition specimen setscontained this classic reverse design in a Specimen finish. These special edition sets ran from 2010 to 2015, but only the 2013-2015 sets contain the classic reverse, since the maple leaf mark didn’t exist before 2012. The composition was bronze plated nickel.
Between 2014 and 2022, silver dollar proof sets contained the classic reverse design in a proof finish. The composition was brass plated steel. The 2023 set also had the classic reverse design, but used the double dated obverse for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.
In 2024, the use of the classic reverse design continued with the new obverse for King Charles III. 2024 was the only year this design, effigy, and composition combination was used for a proof set, as there have been no silver dollar proof sets released since.
Note that the multi-coin silver proof sets, which contain pure silver coins (unlike the silver dollar proof sets, which contain only a dollar), also used the ‘classic reverse’ design, including the Queen Elizabeth II, ‘in the name of Queen Elizabeth II’, and King Charles IIIsilver proof sets.

In 2012, the Mint transitioned to a new loonie designwhich featured a maple leaf security mark. This new security mark did not get added to loonies found in proof and specimen sets. Instead, a 'classic reverse' design was used, which did not use the new maple leaf mark.
Between 2013 and 2015, special edition specimen setscontained this classic reverse design in a Specimen finish. These special edition sets ran from 2010 to 2015, but only the 2013-2015 sets contain the classic reverse, since the maple leaf mark didn’t exist before 2012. The composition was bronze plated nickel.
Between 2014 and 2022, silver dollar proof sets contained the classic reverse design in a proof finish. The composition was brass plated steel. The 2023 set also had the classic reverse design, but used the double dated obverse for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.
In 2024, the use of the classic reverse design continued with the new obverse for King Charles III. 2024 was the only year this design, effigy, and composition combination was used for a proof set, as there have been no silver dollar proof sets released since.
Note that the multi-coin silver proof sets, which contain pure silver coins (unlike the silver dollar proof sets, which contain only a dollar), also used the ‘classic reverse’ design, including the Queen Elizabeth II, ‘in the name of Queen Elizabeth II’, and King Charles IIIsilver proof sets.

The Loon dollar exhibits doubling that is shifted in the same direction, the identifying characteristic of Class IV Offset Hub Doubling, which means the hub to die alignment was offset to one side. This type of doubling can occur with single-press hubbing, which was first used for Canadian coins in 1978.
Doubling is perhaps most visible in the words CANADA and DOLLAR and the designer’s initials on the reverse of the coin, which displays the standard Loon dollar design by Robert Ralph-Carmichael.
Trees at the water’s edge also exhibit doubling, and doubling is seen at the left wall of the incuse circle in which the maple leaf security device is found.
Wexler initially believed the doubling on the Loon dollar to be mechanical doubling, but closer inspection “shows a strong notching effect on many of the letters. The doubling on the beads near the rim does appear to be raised and rounded as does the doubling on other fine details such as the small trees and the designer’s initials.”
The final initial in the designer’s initials shows very nice separation of images, he added.
Class I doubling, like that on the famous 1955 Lincoln, Doubled Die Obverse cent, would give a notably different appearance than what is seen on the Loon dollar in the set.
Doubling on $2 coin
Less severe doubling is visible on the $2 coin, especially so in the word ELIZABETH, the year 2013 and the designer’s initials on the shoulder of Susanna Blunt’s effigy of Queen Elizabeth II.
The class of doubling on the $2 coin appears to be the same as on the Loon dollar, Wexler said.

The Canadian Bank of Commerce issued its first series of bank notes when itopened in 1867. In 1888, the Commerce released another issue of colourful bank notes in various denominations—with security so effective that the series design did not change for almost 30 years.
This coin is the first of an exciting new series celebrating the art and evolution of bank note designin Canada. Don't delay: order yours today!

Your coin features a seascape-themed vignette from the Canadian Bank of Commerce's 1888 20-dollar bank note. The designcentres a youthful figure: possibly a young Hermès, who was a god of the Greek pantheon anda patron of travellers. The figure leans on a large fish, holding a staff entwined by two snakes. Also known as a caduceus, this staff symbolizes commerce and balance. In the background are four ships from various ages of sea travel, a rocky point juttingout into the water, and a tall lighthouse to guide the vessels to safe harbour.
The coin's reverse also features the word "CANADA,"the date "2013" and the face value of "5 DOLLARS."

Over the last three centuries, the evolution of paper currency in Canada has involved a highly specialized art form and human technology, set against the backdrop of ever-changing economics. The Canadian Bank of Commerce issued its first series of bank notes when itopened in 1867. Your coin features a seascape-themed vignette from the Canadian Bank of Commerce's 1888 20-dollar bank note. The designcentres a youthful figure: possibly a young Hermès, who was a god of the Greek pantheon anda patron of travellers. The figure leans on a large fish, holding a staff entwined by two snakes. Also known as a caduceus, this staff symbolizes commerce and balance. In the background are four ships from various ages of sea travel, a rocky point juttingout into the water, and a tall lighthouse to guide the vessels to safe harbour.

The coin with the highest mintage in 2013 was the Canadian **$1 “loonie.”**
